newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Lyonnaise board backs merger, terms not fixed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lyonnaise board backs merger, terms not fixed.

text.p: French utilities group Lyonnaise des Eaux on Thursday said its board had backed a merger with holding company Cie de Suez in principle but no terms had been fixed.

Among issues to be agreed ahead of board meetings of the two companies on April 11 to discuss a merger are the share parities and the amount of any exceptional dividend made to Suez shareholders ahead of a merger.
Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod said the idea of a merger with Suez was an "excellent plan" but no terms had been finalised yet.
"The terms have not been fixed in any way whatsoever," he told a news conference held to present Lyonnaise 1996 results.

One industry source said the fact that Suez and Lyonnaise had been forced to call special board meetings to discuss the merger, rather than approving them at board meetings this week, suggested they still had work to do in sorting out the terms of a deal.

They have to steer a fine line between making their alliance work and satisfying Suez shareholders, who are asking for an exceptional dividend payout as a sweetener in return for their backing for the merger.

So far Suez has said only that it will make an exceptional dividend payment to reflect capital gains made on the sale of investment bank Banque Indosuez last year but has declined to specify the amount.
Monod said any exceptional dividend payment would affect the parity between Lyonnaise and Suez shares in a merger.
"The principle is clear. If there is an exceptional dividend payment, it will have an impact on the parity," he told a news conference.
Saint Gobain chief Jean-Louis Beffa suggested on Tuesday a payout equivalent to 3.4 billion francs ($600 million).
He said his call for an exceptional dividend was shared by other Suez shareholders including insurer Axa-UAP and bank Banque Nationale de Paris.
Axa and BNP have so far declined comment.
Monod said Lyonnaise was actively seeking partners in France or beyond to become a major player in the European telecommunications sector.

Analysts believe Lyonnaise would use Suez's cash pile and potential to generate new cash through asset sales to fund its own expansion. Suez, meanwhile, is looking for a new identity, having sold many of its key assets, including Banque Indosuez.
Earlier Lyonnaise said it made a net attributable profit last year of 1.35 billion francs, compared with 906 million in 1995, on sales of 91.6 billion, up from 85.8 billion.
Analysts had said they expected a net attributable profit for 1996 of between 1.0 and 1.5 billion francs.
Lyonnaise said it was looking forward to further growth in business and profitability during 1997.
